scenario: A workflow deploys to App Service using a publish profile stored as a repository secret.
options: Rotate the publish profile monthly
Use azure/login with OIDC: grant id-token: write and configure a federated credential on an Azure identity scoped to the target
Store the publish profile in an environment variable instead
Use the owner's personal Azure credentials
explanation: OIDC federation lets the job exchange a GitHub-signed token for an Azure token, so no long-lived credential is stored anywhere. Rotating or relocating a secret keeps the problem, and personal credentials tie deployments to one person.

scenario: The production deployment identity's federated credential trusts any workflow in the shop-api repository.
stem: Why should its subject be repo:shop/shop-api:environment:production instead?
options: It makes deployments faster
Only jobs running in the production environment - after its protection rules pass - can obtain the production identity, not pull requests or feature branches
It is required for staging
It removes the need for an Azure subscription ID
explanation: The subject is what Entra checks before issuing a token. Tying it to the production environment means the environment's reviewers and branch rules gate access to production credentials. A repository-wide subject lets any job in any branch act as production.

scenario: The production environment requires a reviewer, but someone triggered the workflow manually from a feature branch and the reviewer approved without noticing the branch.
stem: Which setting would have blocked it?
options: A longer wait timer
Deployment branch rules on the production environment allowing only main (or release tags)
More reviewers
A different runner
explanation: Deployment branch rules stop jobs from other branches using the environment at all, regardless of how the workflow was triggered. Reviewers and timers still depend on a person noticing.

scenario: A workflow uses a popular third-party action referenced as @v4. The action's maintainer account is compromised and the v4 tag is moved to malicious code.
stem: What would have protected the workflow?
options: Using @master instead
Pinning the action to a full commit SHA and updating it deliberately, for example with Dependabot
Running the workflow less often
Using a Windows runner
explanation: Tags and branches can be moved to different code; a commit SHA cannot. Pinning means the workflow runs exactly the reviewed code, and updates arrive as reviewable pull requests. This happened for real in 2025, leaking secrets from thousands of repositories.

stem: What should a workflow's top-level permissions usually be?
options: write-all, so every step can do what it needs
contents: read, with additional permissions such as id-token: write granted only to the jobs that need them
No permissions block, since the defaults are always safe
admin
explanation: The GITHUB_TOKEN can push code, create releases and more if allowed. Least privilege at the top, widened per job, limits what a compromised or misbehaving step can do. Defaults vary by organisation settings and should not be relied on.

scenario: A workflow step runs: echo "Building ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}". An attacker opens a pull request whose title contains shell commands.
stem: What is the problem and the fix?
options: No problem; titles are escaped automatically
The title is inserted into the script and executed; pass untrusted values through environment variables and treat them as data
Pull request titles cannot contain special characters
Use a macOS runner
explanation: Expressions are substituted into the script text before the shell runs it, so a crafted title becomes code. Assigning it to an environment variable and referencing the variable keeps it as data. This is a well-known Actions pitfall.

scenario: Four repositories contain nearly identical 150-line deploy workflows that have slowly drifted apart.
stem: What should the platform team provide?
options: A wiki page with the recommended YAML
A reusable workflow in a platform repository that each repository calls with workflow_call
A fifth copy with the latest changes
One workflow file shared by symbolic link
explanation: Reusable workflows keep deploy logic in one place, so fixes and security improvements reach every caller. Documentation and copies drift, and Git repositories cannot share files by link.

scenario: An open-source repository from the shop wants faster builds using a self-hosted runner on the office network.
options: Self-hosted runners cannot run Node
Anyone can open a pull request to a public repository, so their code could run on a machine inside the office network
Self-hosted runners cost more minutes
Public repositories cannot use runners
explanation: Workflows triggered by pull requests run the contributor's code on the runner. On a public repository that means strangers executing code inside your network. Use GitHub-hosted or larger runners for public repositories.
